Research pilot

Keep the thinking yours.

Most work with AI runs on one loop: you ask, you wait, it answers. Does that shape quietly make handing over your thinking the easy default? Reckon is a research pilot trying to find out, and rethinking the interaction itself so that thinking with AI feels rewarding and stays visibly your own.

A few words is enough to start.

A sketch of a feeling, not a product feature. It runs in your browser with a few fixed word rules and pre-written answers. No AI is called, nothing you type leaves this page, and nothing is stored or measured.

The question

Ask. Wait. Answer. Repeat.

Nobody sets out to stop thinking. So what does the turn-taking itself do? If each exchange centers on the answer, when does your own reasoning get a turn of its own?

  1. 01

    Ask

    What if the question leaves your hands while it is still half-formed? Does the half you had not worked out yet get skipped?

  2. 02

    Wait

    What if the wait is where the problem slips away? When the answer lands, are you still holding it, or reading it cold?

  3. 03

    Answer

    Does a finished-looking reply invite a yes more than a judgment? And does your next message get shorter?

These are working hypotheses the pilot is looking into, not settled findings.

The open question

So what could replace the loop? We do not know yet.

Reckon exists to rethink the interaction itself, not to add a feature to the chat box. We have not picked an answer, and nothing on this page is a design we have chosen. The pilot below is how we are learning.

  • What would make thinking with AI feel rewarding, not like extra work?
  • When does taking turns help you think, and does it ever quietly take over?
  • What would you want to see about your own habits, if you could?

What exists today

A small pilot. Software, then a person.

The only live parts today are an open-source collector and findings written by hand. Nothing watches you, and nothing on this page runs on your sessions.

  1. 1

    Run the collector

    One command runs the open-source collector on your machine. It finds your newest local AI sessions.

  2. 2

    A masked copy is uploaded

    Detected key-like values are replaced with stars in a copy, and that copy is uploaded once.

  3. 3

    A person writes findings

    Someone reads your sessions and writes findings by hand: observations and hypotheses, not verdicts.

  4. 4

    You read them privately

    Findings appear on your private page when they are ready. You decide what, if anything, to change.

Get the collector

Plainly

What happens to your sessions

The collector runs on your machine and does not modify your original files. It uploads a copy of the transcript content with detected key-like values replaced by stars. Masking can miss secrets, and names, emails, personal information and code remain readable in the uploaded copy.

  • Masking is deterministic local pattern matching, with no network calls.
  • Your masked copy goes to private storage operated by the person running the pilot. A real person reads it to write your findings. It is not sold, shared, or made public.
  • The pilot allows one upload per account, with small caps on accounts and upload size.
  • The collector code is public, so you can read exactly what runs and what leaves your machine.

Self-serve deletion and automatic retention limits are not built into this pilot yet. It is run by one operator, the person who gave you the install command.

What it is not

Nothing to score. Nothing to watch.

  • No scores
  • No rankings
  • No productivity surveillance
  • No dashboard
